Together with representatives of the HVO government, certain conclusions were reached ..." The text is not legible. It's a poor copy, so I can only guess what it says.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. You read the passage that is important. You see that this document refers to those discussions that you had with the HVO representatives. The document comes from the Vitez Brigade command. Here's my question: Do you feel that the report gives a true description of the negotiating conditions that existed during those negotiations with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Well, the report is correct and detailed. It is true that we attended those negotiations, but it doesn't say that we were detained. It is all correct. All that is missing is the fact that we were detained.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were not free at the time of those negotiations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: We were not free.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness L, you spent several days in the cinema building in Vitez, along with several hundred other detainees. When you were in those premises, were you subjected to interrogations by the civilian police, and then with ten other detainees, you were forced to dig trenches in the Vranjska and Rijeka region around 6.00 or 7.00?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the area where you had to dig those trenches, were you being guarded by soldiers who were wearing camouflage uniforms, among whom you recognised some of them as coming from Vitez or Rijeka?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, I recognised a couple of them, and they were wearing camouflage uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did you see Mario Cerkez there while you were in detention?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Once or twice, I did see him.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The end of April 1993, did you see the chief of the BH army coming in, that is, General Halilovic, who was accompanied by the chief of the HVO, General Petkovic, and did you also see that Mario Cerkez was there when those two people came in?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, Mario was there too.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was it stated at that time that all the detainees would be released but that you yourself wanted to be released with a group of people from the neighbourhood of Stari Vitez, that is, Old Vitez? And at the moment when you thought you would be released, a soldier said to you that you could not be released because you were not from Stari Vitez.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This soldier, was his name Anto Kovac, who was known as Zabac, that is, "the frog" in your language?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Also while you were kept in detention, since you were not released in the end, is it true that another soldier came to get you and took you to the office of the accused, Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Was that soldier Ratko Nuk?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In Mario Cerkez's office, in addition to Mario Cerkez himself, did you meet Mr. Pero Skopljak?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: During the meeting, which was rather short, Mr. Skopljak showed you a document which came from Mate Boban; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: And the document authorised you to conduct negotiations; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I don't know. I understood the question differently from the interpretation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The question was perhaps not well-translated in English; that's possible. Anything is possible. The document in question did not authorise you to conduct negotiations but rather it authorised Mr. Skopljak to conduct the negotiations.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the end, you refused to continue the conversation with Mr. Skopljak; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I said that I wasn't authorised to negotiate on behalf of Central Bosnia or Vitez, I wasn't the person who had any authorisation, but that I would negotiate if I was authorised to do so.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did Mr. Skopljak or possibly the accused, Mario Cerkez, who is here in this courtroom, did they tell you what the purpose of those negotiations were supposed to be?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Probably the situation, which was extremely tense in the area of Central Bosnia, probably the aim was to try and find some solutions.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: In the end, a few days later, that is, in early May 1993, you yourself and other detainees who had remained at the cinema were transferred initially to the chess club building where you spent a night, and then you were transferred to the Kaonik camp; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, as regards what happened at the Kaonik camp, this appears in the summary which was given to you. If the Trial Chamber wishes us to speak about those facts with the witness, I'm prepared to do so, but if you prefer that we move more quickly, since this witness has already testified about those facts as part of the Aleksovski case, then I am prepared to suggest to the Trial Chamber that it simply take into account the transcript which was prepared at that time. I will do as you instruct me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be more simple, rather than putting a transcript in at this stage, to ask the witness a few questions about what happened in Kaonik, bearing in mind that we've heard much evidence on this topic already.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness L, do you therefore confirm that you were transferred, that you were detained for about two weeks at the Kaonik camp in May 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is it true that during that detention, on several occasions, you were interrogated either in the camp or in facilities in Busovaca?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Is it also true that during that period, you were mistreated by guards in the camp, particularly by one whose name was Svabo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, just that one guard. Not other guards, but that one guard.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Did he also threaten you with a knife?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Do you remember that one day, that same guard, after having struck you, made a phone call and said to the person he was speaking with, "Chief, everything's fine. I've finished my job"?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Were you finally released from Kaonik camp on the 14th of May, 1993, that you were taken back to the Vitez cinema and exchanged two days later?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Before you were released, were you asked whether you wanted to stay in Vitez or whether, on the contrary, you preferred to leave?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, I was asked that.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: What was your choice, Witness L?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I said that I would not stay in Vitez but that I would go to Zenica. It was unsafe in Vitez, at least that was my assumption.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could I have a few moments, Mr. President? Excuse me.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Excuse me for that short interruption, Mr. President. I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Who is going to begin the cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, counsel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honours. We did not discuss that issue. Whatever seems to be more practical.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Perhaps you would like to have a word with Mr. Sayers.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, we would.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Might I suggest, Your Honour, that if we could take our break early, I might have the opportunity to consult with my client, and that will accelerate very greatly the proceedings.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Would the President turn his microphone on, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It wouldn't be convenient, as far as I'm concerned, to take the break then because I've got a meeting which I've fixed to fit in with our current arrangements. Can you and Mr. Kovacic have a quick word to decide what to do?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes. Could we just have two minutes here?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Your Honours, we agreed that the Cerkez Defence will go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could I also suggest that, a technical detail, I move over to the place of Mr. Naumovski because from here, we don't see each other, the witness and I. I'm sorry for wasting your time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Good afternoon. My name is Bozidar Kovacic. I'm an attorney from Rijeka, not your Rijeka, the other Rijeka, and together with my colleague, Mikulicic, we represent the accused, Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could we ask counsel to speak into the microphone, please?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, please, very briefly, by way of introduction, to save time, you knew Mario Cerkez before the conflict of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, he worked in the SPS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any private contact outside of work?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, we knew each other. It's a small place.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have any common friends?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Certainly, we did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever have any disputes with him?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: No, never.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Either at work or outside of work, through your contacts, did you ever have occasion to notice a segregational approach towards other religions and other ethnic groups?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: He worked in a different department so that my contacts with him were not frequent, nor did I have occasion to notice anything at all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you ever hear of him advocating such views?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: No, I never heard anything along those lines.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In view of the size of the community you lived in, do you believe you would have heard if he had such views?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness L --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I apologise. I used the name, but it was rather -- how shall I say --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: The interpreter didn't --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Nobody else heard it. We heard it as "Witness L."

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm sorry. It was a slip of the tongue.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness L, from the summary that we received an hour ago from the Prosecution, I learn that you are now in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Assistant Minister for Reconstruction and Development in the cantonal government?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you confirm a few points in that connection? The process of return --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Would it be sensible if this matter went into private session?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I was told, Your Honour, that there are a couple of assistants, so I don't believe that that could --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: It may be more sensible to go into private session. When you go on to another topic, you can tell us and we'll go back into open session.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned the crisis staff and cooperation between both ethnic communities in Vitez, and then we came to the point when, at the crisis staff, it was agreed that a joint operation should be carried out in Slimena, which is in May 1992. You said that you heard from Hakija Cengic that the HVO did not respect the terms of the agreement and, in fact, started the operation two days ahead of time.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: You see, that is the information I received. There are people who know that precisely. Hakija Cengic and Kulenovic, I think he was actually there, and can tell you authentically and emphatically what happened. It is difficult for me now to recollect those details because I didn't participate. I was just informed about it. So it is very difficult for me to say whether it is a question of days or hours, who betrayed whom, and so on. I think if you are really interested in those details, it would be better to talk to those people because they are the ones who informed me about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. So I infer from that that at the crisis staff itself, it was agreed, in principle, to launch this operation, but the military elements of the operation were not discussed.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: You see, the HVO and the TO probably did discuss those things, but we didn't go into those details. I didn't know anything about the army for me to discuss military matters. A general position was taken, but the operative side was implemented by them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I understand. But please confirm if I'm right in saying that at the crisis staff, the need for the operation was agreed and the military would carry out the operation, without going into the details of the operation itself; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You said in some earlier statements that you knew that the operation was led by Filipovic on behalf of the HVO and that Cerkez was one of the leaders of that operation; is that true?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: In view of the fact that the Vitez Brigade participated, and as Cerkez was the commander of the Vitez Brigade, I assume so. Whether he personally was there, whether he personally participated, I wasn't there to tell. There were three municipalities involved, Travnik, Novi Travnik, and so I assumed that Filipovic too must have known because he participated in those talks. But whether Cerkez was there on the spot is something I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Witness L, just for clarification's sake, so it was a joint operation against the Serb aggressor, or, rather, an attack on a warehouse containing weapons which the Yugoslav People's Army had seized from the municipal TOs earlier on.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: A second point. I probably think it was misspoken because in 1992, there was no such unit called the Vitez Brigade. You were thinking of people from Vitez. Because a moment ago, you used the term "Vitez Brigade."

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: The HVO, yes. The HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There was the HVO; that, we agree on. Did you hear anything at all about members of the Territorial Defence participating in the military part of that operation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, they were assigned the task of carrying out that operation. There were some wounded people too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Let me go on to the part when you mentioned --

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, might I intervene just for a moment? Has it been contested that the accused, Mario Cerkez, participated in the attack on Slimena. In front of me, I've got the Defence brief of 6 April, 1999 from the accused in which it says that he participated in that attack.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Counsel is able to ask what the witness knows about that, and the witness says he doesn't know anything himself about it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: By the way, Your Honours, there is no position that Cerkez wasn't attached. What I wanted to clarify was a detail. The impression was that somehow indirectly, it is implied that the HVO acted differently in opposition to what they agreed upon with the army; that is why I asked the witness about that. But that doesn't seem to be the case now.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You told us about the event when the HOS captured the building of the municipality and the police station, and you were the most responsible person in the municipality at the time because Santic was in Zagreb. Is there any doubt at all that that operation was, indeed, carried out by HOS units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: It was them, yes. People who belonged to that unit carried out the attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Was the HOS an extremist force on the Croatian side in Bosnia in those days, in 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Was HOS what?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The extreme wing of the Croatian side in the conflict.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: The question is not clear to me.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: If I may say so, on both sides, the Croatian and the Muslim, there were moderates and there were extremists. When talking about the Croatian side, was the HOS the extremist wing?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: That is what the HVO said.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But from public knowledge, from the events that took place, was that your impression too?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to say which people participated where. That is what they said and that is what it probably was. Who participated in the attack on the MUP, as for the planting of explosives, all we can say is that they were extremists. I can't say whether they were HOS or not. But these are facts, material facts that actually happened. The perpetrators were not identified. All we can say is that they were carried out by extremists. If I knew that they had done it, I would say that they were people from HOS.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell me, Mr. L, you know that later on, HOS joined the HVO and ceased to exist formally as the HOS.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you know that the leader or the commander of the HOS forces in Vitez was a person called Darko Kraljevic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that there were rumours about them, that they were very evil?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, those were the rumours.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Is it true that they had their main stronghold in a part of Vitez called Kolonija, where you lived?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, they were in a cafe. That was their meeting place, yes. It was called Benc, if I'm not mistaken, or 072.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, they are one next to another.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I didn't go there so I don't really know exactly. You're asking me something that I'm assuming, that I heard, that I didn't see.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The HVO government had a custom to blame all incidents on the HOS, or anything that was not in their favour on HOS or other extremists.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For the purpose of verification, did the Muslim side also have problems with its own extremists?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Well, before we deal with that, the time has come to adjourn. You can return to that subject if you want, Mr. Kovacic, at a quarter past two. Witness L, we are going to adjourn till a quarter past two. Would you be back then, please? Meanwhile, don't speak to anybody about your evidence and don't let anybody speak to you about it until it's over. Would you remember that that also includes members of the Prosecution team? Could you be back, please, at 2.15? --- Luncheon recess taken at 12.47 p.m.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Kovacic.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness L, we left off at the question, if you will recall, whether there were any extremists on the Muslim side.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: It would be stupid to say that there are no extremists in some ethnic groups. It is just the way they are indoctrinated. Are you putting out fires with water or gasoline? So that, in a way, is the answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, you mentioned Mr. Ivica Santic, as far as I know, he was a good friend of yours.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I considered him to have been a good friend of mine.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: There was a story that at one point, he hid you in his house in order to protect you from these extremists.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: In fact, others interpreted it that way. We had some conversations and talks. His house was about 50 to 100 metres away from where I lived there, and I went over there, I spent the night, in order to have a lengthy conversation, so we could do something. This was this period in October.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can I infer from that that both of you, as men and as politicians, cooperated and looked for solutions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: At that time, yes, I believe that was the case, in 1992. I made an effort and I believe he did make an effort too.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. When you gave evidence, you mentioned, with respect to your detention in the cinema building, certain HVO persons. Anto Kovac, called Zabac, and Ratko Nuk, who were bodyguards or escorts of Cerkez, they were members of the military police; right?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I assume so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you perhaps notice any insignia which would identify them as military policemen or just the fact --

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I'm afraid that I did not pay attention to any details. It is possible that that was the case.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You also said that you don't know any details about the internal organisation structure of the army, the HVO or the BH army.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I may have known a little bit more about the BH army.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that within the HVO, there are different units?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Probably. I guess. Probably.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Do you agree with me that in the Vitez area, in late 1992 and during the conflict which started in 1993, there were also units present which had come from outside of Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I did receive such information.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. You mentioned previously, and I would like to verify that, that Mario Cerkez was the HVO commander in May of 1992. Did you have in mind that he was one of the key people in the HVO in 1992, and do you know his precise position?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: It is hard for me to place him in this hierarchy, where he was inside the HVO. I don't know what importance he was. I don't know whether he was the fifth or sixth in rank, or second or third. I know he was not the first. That, I know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can we clarify this a bit further, please? By your position, did you attend the crisis staff meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes. They were held in the municipality and this is where I worked.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In 1992, did Mario Skopljak come there as a representative of the military component of the HVO, to those meetings?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: In this initial phase, these armed forces -- that is, not the TO. This was not in 1991; this was in 1992, maybe in April 1992, maybe even March 1992. Perhaps it was March. We had representatives of the Patriotic League as members of the crisis staff.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, did this military component of the HVO have the name of HVO headquarters? Do you know that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I really don't recall that. I really don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But could you confirm that Mario Skopljak did attend those meetings in that period?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And you are unable to say what his position was?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: No, not precisely. I know that he represented the HVO. I don't know which component. The Patriotic League and the HVO at that time, in January, February, and March, they were not legitimate at that time yet.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can you recall any meeting of the crisis staff, or some other meeting where critical issues were being discussed, that Mario Skopljak and Cerkez attended together? We're talking about 1992, of course.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: You mean in a meeting?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I cannot recall this. There were 10, 12, sometimes 14 people present there, so I cannot.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. If you cannot, you cannot. Thank you. In that period of 1992, the relationship between the Croatians and the Muslims was -- Hakija Cengic was the leader of the Territorial Defence, and parallel to him, Marijan Skopljak on the Croatian side. Was that the case? Does that ring any bells for you?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: No, I cannot tell you anything about that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. You mentioned, that is, we saw this press release of the Committee for the Protection of Muslims -- in fact, there were two of them -- but my question is, did anybody of the authorities issue any formal decision banning the Committee for the Protection of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: No. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So the authorities did not prevent the activities of this committee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this committee was active as late as October 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: What about the Patriotic League? When was it changed into the Patriotic League?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: You see, the Patriotic League was established in late 1991 and it was active through 1992. This was in June/July 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When was the war presidency established?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: In January 1993.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So at the time when this committee ceased to exist.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: There may have been a vacuum for about a month or two.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In October 1992, we are referring to the 19th and 20th of October, you mentioned this meeting which was attended by Ivica Santic and Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: They showed up at the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they come to the headquarters?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, they came to the headquarters.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: At that time, there were already barricades, the two which you mentioned on the main road. What was the purpose of their coming?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Primarily, to have those barricades removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: How did you perceive this? As a constructive attempt to resolve the problem about the erection of the barricades?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: The barricades had been put up in order to prevent those units from entering Vitez. The conflict had already broken out in Novi Travnik.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mean, not in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Not in Vitez, but they were supposed to pass through Vitez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: According to this document, you know that the erection of the barricades was ordered by the 3rd Corps command.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: That is possible, yes, because this army already had a hierarchy, a chain of command, and so probably the commander was the one who had ordered it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. So we agree that at that time there was an active conflict going on in Novi Travnik. At that time, there was also fighting in Jajce in October of 1992?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In Jajce, Croats and Muslims fought together against the Serbs?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When the barricade was removed, the BiH army's interpretation was that the barricade would prevent the Croatian troops from going through Vitez and move on to Novi Travnik, from the standpoint of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: You are asking me what the thinking was of the 3rd Corps? Perhaps they had a more different strategic point of view, but myself, as a citizen of Vitez and as a member of the local government, I wanted to see that the units did not enter Vitez, that we didn't have further problems. As far as the 3rd Corps is concerned, for their decisions, you need to ask them.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. But in looking for solutions in order to prevent the conflict from coming to your town, is it true that Santic also endeavoured to find a solution, and he suggested that the HVO troops be let to pass through but not stay on in town.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Well, that is very uncertain. You don't know if you can -- difficult to implement. But this is not an expert opinion of mine, and I think you need to ask the military people for that.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But were there such suggestions?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Since Santic and Cerkez were representing Croats, who was the person who was actually conducting talks? Was it Santic or Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I believe that it was Santic who was leading the conversation, and Cerkez was there as the brigade commander. So there it was.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: As a military person?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But he did not take part in the negotiations, in the conversations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: He just was trying to have the barricades removed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So you allow the possibility of this being discussed as a way, as a solution to the problem, to let them pass through but not let them stay. Was that then discarded as technically not viable?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: This is the position that I took. This is how I saw it.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. As a public official, as a politician at that time, would you agree with me that, despite the fact that the conflict had already broken out in other parts of Bosnia -- we're talking about early 1993 now; in other places in Bosnia, conflicts were already in progress -- is it true that politicians in Vitez, all of them tried to find ways to keep the status quo?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I don't know if we can say that all of them did, but a majority of those with whom I had any dealings did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree that the incidents which took place in your town in late 1992 and early 1993, which mostly had affected the Muslims, that people still managed to prevent this from conflagrating into a general conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, we did continue to meet, even though sometimes there were no concrete results, but we tried to keep the communication channels open all the time.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Would you agree with me that in the period of late 1992 and early 1993, the situation was so complex and so tense that any incident along ethnic lines could have produced a conflagration at that time, at that moment when it happened?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Well, there were conflicts, and if you take this logic -- and, as you put it, there were those conflicts and those frictions, and I believe that we needed to be patient, regardless of all the problems.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When looking for solutions, you said something in one of your statements previously, do you recall the meetings when you tried to look for a solution, you mentioned today when you would have two armies working together, that there was even an idea of forming an HMVO, where there would be both Croats and Muslims?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, there were such ideas.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Were the people who were proposed for that people who were irrelevant or -- the people who were proposed for that, were they irrelevant people or were they people who didn't carry much influence?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Well, I'd say that they were relevant to a degree, and some of these ideas were forwarded to Grude, but they were not accepted. If we had even proposed it, even though we were bypassing the law a little bit, we even contemplated breaking the law to a degree, in an effort to prevent the conflict, but we did not succeed.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You mentioned when people were given documents about the reorganisation of jobs and that 10 or 12 Muslims were let go; you mentioned their names too. You were part of the municipal government. Let's see first how many people were employed in the local government.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: About 100.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I assume that in terms of ethnic structure, 80 to 90 per cent was divided between the Muslims and the Croats.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, there was a balance. We have inherited that situation, and this had been the case previously, and now just new party appointees were brought into this place, but there was a balance. I think we had found a balanced situation before we came into power -- when we came into power.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: When the power was shared, this had nothing to do with the election results, and you inherited the bureaucratic structure, which had nothing to do with the election results; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But the situation which you found in terms of staff, it reflected the structure of the population in town?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, it did.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In other words, you will agree with me that approximately out of 50 Muslim employees, 10 were fired?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, even though I shouldn't have been fired without a decision of the entire assembly and that nobody can fire me unless there is a decision of the entire assembly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So among the employees, how many appointees were there and how many were just permanently employed?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Three or four were appointees which were appointed by the parliament, and the rest were just hired on a permanent basis.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So 10 to 12 employees of Muslim ethnic background were fired because they refused to sign the new document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And out of them, three or four, give or take two, three or four were fired who had been appointees?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: That is not what I'm trying to say. If these appointees were also given this document to sign, that is pretty illegal.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Other witnesses have stated that the SDA party had taken a position on this?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, the party did take positions on certain issues, and a number of those, 20 or 30 decisions, were taken. I don't know exactly how many.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Right. You said that even you had been offered a position in the new HVO government and you refused it. Did you refuse it on the basis of the position of the party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: In principle, I need to be guided by the position of the party, but it was also illegal, and as a member of the parliament, I thought that I also needed to follow the law.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I now want to take you to the period immediately preceding the 16th of April, 1993. You mentioned the meeting of 15 April, 1993 with the representatives of the BH army, and you were present where there was the HVO meeting with the BH army representatives on the eve of the conflict. Would you agree with me that immediately before the conflict, tensions had obviously risen significantly?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Certain things need to be experienced. There was something in the air; it was hovering. You simply are expecting something. It is hard to explain. It's something in the air. I don't know if there is a physical manifestation, but the situation is such.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So were these meetings held in order to try to resolve the situation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Are you referring to the meeting of the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Well, yes, there was a committee, relatively speaking, where representatives of the Muslim and Croatian population met, the police and military structures. I was a member of the presidency. I didn't call it, but I was present, and all these people were called, even some members of the presidency, and this situation, this atmosphere was discussed and they gave their position. They said that there would not be any conflict, all three of them mentioned this, and they said there would not be a meeting and they said that they would meet there again tomorrow even. So Sahabudin Muratovic, Sefkija Dzidic, and Safet Sivro, all three of them said so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did they express that as their own position or did they do it after a meeting with the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: You have to ask them. I cannot say that on their behalf. They may have had intelligence, they may have had meetings, I just don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But let me ask you simply, from what they said, did it imply that they had had contacts and conversations with their counterparts in the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, that is how it seemed. I think that there was even an argument put forward that there was another meeting called for the next day, so if there was another meeting called for the next day, there would be nothing happening.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. Do you know whether, on the 14th of April, there was a celebration of the anniversary of the BH army?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you see any representatives of the HVO attending these celebrations?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, there was Mr. Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So this was on the 14th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, two days before the conflict.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And he came as a representative of the HVO?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On that critical morning, on the 16th, you heard the shooting, and there were all kinds of things going on. Would you agree with me, or would you deny the assessment that at least in this part of the town in which you lived, that is, Kolonija, that for the first two or three days of the conflict, the situation was chaotic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: It was rather, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The troops roaming around the streets, whose presence was very visible, was it clear which units those troops belonged to, who was responsible to whom?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: It is difficult for me to tell. All I can say is that I saw a couple of neighbours. While I was on this side of the building, I saw them, but I can't tell you the exact insignia or anything like that. At least the first morning, it was something I didn't look at. I had other problems on my mind, to get away from it all.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Tell us, can you inform us whether uniforms were different, whether there were various uniforms?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, there were camouflage and black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In those days, but also before and after, can we consider a uniform to be a distinctive sign as to which troops a soldier belonged to, until we see the insignia?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I don't understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: For example, did the HVO troops wear only one type of uniform?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: They mostly wore camouflage uniforms. There may have been some small differences, but it was difficult for me to notice those differences. If you're thinking of the shade of colour of the camouflage uniform or that sort of thing --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: No. I'm asking whether within the HVO, there were people wearing black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I did see a couple of people wearing black uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But you don't know who they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On some occasions at least, did the military police of the HVO wear some kind of sign by which they could be distinguished?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I think they wore those white belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: The classical kind of belts that were worn in the former system by the JNA troops?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could you clarify a point for us? We went through it rather quickly today and I think it's rather important. It emerged that you were captured and taken to the cinema. You made a statement to the court investigators in July 1995, on the 21st and 22nd of July, 1995, and in talking about those events, you actually said, and I shall quote, "The plan was for Fadil to attract the attention of two HVO members whom he knew while I would run off to the lorry and mix with the other Muslims who were being taken to the cinema. The plan succeeded and I was taken to the cinema." So to speed things up, as I understand it, this means that you intentionally joined a group that was being taken somewhere because you felt safer in a large group than as an individual on the road.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I felt that if they found me in my apartment, I would be liquidated, and so I thought that if I had a chance, it was within a large group. Because if you wish to kill someone from a large group, you have to take him out and everyone will see it, so it's more complicated. So I thought if I was to survive, it was best for me to be within a larger group. But they were collecting all Bosniaks from Vitez and they would have reached me too. They did search the apartment several times in which I lived.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I'm not saying that the cinema was a pleasant experience, but it gave you a certain measure of security.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Well, you see, this was how I reasoned: I thought that if somebody wanted to do something against me, he was as intelligent as me, and if he wanted to do it, he would take me out of a group. So I had a chance if I stayed within the group.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: I see. You said that you were listed when you reached the cinema. Was it visible that the military police was doing those lists?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I think that they wore white belts.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Later on, you were taken to the chess club. Was this again done by the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, I think so.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then they took you in a van to Kaonik. Was this again done by the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I assume so, but I'm not quite certain. You see, it's rather difficult to tell in those circumstances.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then again you were taken from Kaonik to the cinema when you were released. Again was this by the military police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I'm afraid I don't know. I couldn't say. The atmosphere is quite specific. Certain details that don't affect you don't stick in your memory when other things are on your mind.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me now go on to the next area, that is, the meeting that you described Mujezinovic, yourself, and others. We're still in the cinema now. Sometime around the 22nd, the 24th, Boro Jozic, Zvonko Cilic, yourself, Mujezinovic, and others, this conversation started. Did you see any chance of this producing some sort of a result in the sense of calming down the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: By nature, I am a person who will always favour negotiations if there is any chance of them being productive, even though there are negotiations when it is difficult, to be quite frank, but I think it's absurd to talk when you are imprisoned. But I accepted everything because I thought there might be a chance of achieving something.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So then as things developed overnight, you required a higher level of negotiators?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I personally know these two persons, I knew what their duties were, and I knew that they were not the persons who could decide. They probably received instructions as to what they should do. If you want to achieve something effective, then you have to look for somebody who has the necessary weight.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: So that is why you wanted to negotiate with Santic, in view of his position as president of the municipality.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, I knew him, and it was easier for me to communicate with him than with others.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But also his position was important?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, certainly, his position was very important. He headed the HVO.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: You also asked for Pero Skopljak, in view of his position as head of the party?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: This story ended with the issuance of a joint statement.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I would like to ask the Court, with Your Honours' permission, to show the witness Z852 [as interpreted]. This is something that has already been admitted into evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness L, would you look through this document? I only have one question for you or, rather, two.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, could we see the document in question, please?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes. I'm not sure that it has been produced, 852 --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Document 752.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm sorry, 752.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Could I check whether the witness has the correct one?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Witness L, have you had a chance to review the document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I think that this document, as far as I can remember, this document was different, but you should ask Mujezinovic. I think that the first point was to respect the International Red Cross, of course, to halt hostilities. Explicitly, reference was made to respect for the agreement between Izetbegovic and Boban. I know that Muhamed signed something outside this agreement, but you must ask him.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Let me just remind you, from the introductory sentence, that is how this was presented to us, that this was a document compiled as a joint statement by the two parties after the agreement which you are referring to was signed. So this is one of the results of that agreement, a joint communique.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I don't know how this statement came into being, but what I attended had these three points. There were other proposals and pressures, but the substance of that document was, point 1, to respect the rules of the International Red Cross; second, to halt hostilities between the army and the HVO; and the third point, that the Izetbegovic-Boban agreement should be respected. That was the gist of that document.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Regardless of the unequal negotiating position of the two parties, because, as you said, you were detainees, the document that you agreed upon eventually, what you have just referred to, would you have signed it under normal conditions as well?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Can I infer from that that the existing inequality, the fact that you were detained, did not have a causal effect on that document that you agreed upon?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: It did not.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I mean, the two are not connected. I agree with the points contained in the document, those that were accepted, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Could the witness be shown a document that was produced today during the examination-in-chief? Document Z751.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Mr. L, I should like to draw your attention, on this occasion, to the last paragraph, which was mentioned earlier on, the sentence which, unfortunately, is illegible in the Croatian version, but it is the one-but-last row. "The government of the HVO ..." Can you find it? In any event, in this document, which is a report issued by the officer on duty in the brigade, and he's sending it to the command of the Operative Zone, mentioning various events that they noticed in the course of the day, he notes that in the building of the Vitez Brigade, this meeting was held and explicit mention is made of representatives of the HVO Vitez government. Would you agree with this, in view of what we have just discussed, that Mujezinovic, you, and others conducted those talks with representatives of the civilian HVO structure, with whom you finally signed your three-point agreement?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I don't know, but, look, look here, I spoke to the president of the HVO government, Santic, and with the president of the HDZ, Pero Skopljak. Now you're asking me something else, and I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Very well. I apologise. Did you negotiate with Cerkez over that document?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Cerkez was not present, except for Cilic --

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: In the first contact.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I think they were present. They were present.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. In your -- rather, I must rephrase that question. We said that you gave statements to the investigators in July 1995, the investigators of this Tribunal, and at one point, when referring to your stay in the cinema building, this must have been in the three or four days before you were transferred, "Several days after I had arrived at the cinema, the civilian HVO police arrived and interrogated me. Sucic and Lazarevic were the men who interrogated me." Is that correct, that you were interrogated by the civilian police?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Thank you. The building in which you were detained, it is known as the cinema building, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: To be more precise, it is the building of the Workers' University.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, it is also known as the Workers' University building, and there was a cinema hall inside. You were tenants or users of premises there. There was a cinema used as an institution; right? There must have been an office in addition to the cinema hall itself. Then there was a cafe during the time of the conflict in the entrance, a coffee-shop. Then there was the headquarters of the Vitez Brigade upstairs on the floor. You said you were with Skopljak in Cerkez's office.

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I think that was downstairs, not in the upstairs.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then there was the Vitez Television offices?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Possibly.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you call that building the building of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: What do you mean?

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: We said that people referred to it as the cinema, as the Workers' University. What else? Was it also referred to as the Vitez Brigade building because it had its headquarters there?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: How do I know? They had their headquarters in the hotel. Maybe it was safer there because we were detained there, so they moved. But I know that their headquarters were in the hotel.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Then you were called to a meeting with Pero Skopljak, you said, and you said that this was in Cerkez's office, and you didn't know until then that it was his office. Was Cerkez present at the meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, he was sitting at the table.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Did you have a cup of coffee?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes, and I started a second cup and I left it unfinished.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Who was a participant in that meeting?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Also present, there was me, Cerkez, and Pero Skopljak.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And that's all? No one else?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Which were the parties? You on one side, obviously, and on the other? Was your collocutor Pero Skopljak in the first place or Mario Cerkez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I don't know how things would have developed. In any event, there were certain exchanges, and then later Pero Skopljak showed me a paper authorising him on talks on Central Bosnia by Boban. I said that I wasn't authorised, I wasn't the authorised person, and that I couldn't continue these discussions, so that the talk was abruptly broken off.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: On the basis of your statement that you were not authorised?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: But I did say that if I was authorised, then -- and I said who could authorise me. There was the president of the party in Vitez, that was the local level and beyond. Since I did participate often and regularly in talks, I said that if they elected me, I could participate. I could not authorise myself.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Please confirm or deny. My understanding is that at the beginning of the meeting, it was established who had the authority, who had the competence. Whoever showed that had -- Skopljak said that he had this document from Boban, that he was authorised and you did not, and then the meeting was broken off. In the course of that meeting, did Cerkez declare his formal position in those talks at all? Did he represent anyone? Was he authorised by anyone?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Well, he was a commander. He was a commander.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: But did he take part in this official part, formal part of the talks when Skopljak presented his authorisation?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: He did not comment. There were some comments before that, but at that point, he had no comments.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: And this was the only formal part of the meeting, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Possibly, yes. I don't know what would have happened if the meeting had continued.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: Yes, we agree. But before that, the small exchanges -- only small exchanges took place; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. KOVACIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, thank you. I have no further questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Your Honour, Mr. Kordic has no questions for this witness. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Sayers, before you finish, let me just look at something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: We want to clarify your position about the telephone conversation. Our recollection is that some other evidence has been given about it, and perhaps you can remind us what your position was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: Yes. Actually, Your Honour, it can be found on page 3758 of the transcript at lines 18 to 25 and 3759, lines 1 to 2, and that was on June the 15th of this year, and then we clarified the position on page 3796, lines 2 to 8. As far as I can see, the testimony given by Witness L is precisely the position that we had represented to the Court, and, therefore, we have no questions for him about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: You have no dispute with that evidence.

utterances.speaker: MR. SAYERS
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Very well. Thank you. Mr. Lopez-Terres?

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have a few clarifications I would like to ask Witness L.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Witness L, first of all, regarding the meeting that you had with the commanders of the BH army in Vitez on the 15th of April, you stated that Mr. Dzidic, Mr. Sivro were there, and you also spoke with Sahabudin Mahmutovic. Sahabudin Mahmutovic, was he a civilian authority or a military authority in Vitez?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: He was the head of the civilian police.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: He was a commander of the civilian police. He didn't have any authority in military matters; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: The meeting of the 15th of April, did it take place when festivities were being organised for the anniversary of the BH army, or was it another meeting in which those three people participated with HVO people?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: The celebration had nothing to do with it.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: So the celebrations had taken place before that then, on the 15th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Are you sure about that point?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes. I think the celebration had nothing to do with the conversation which -- the talks which they had with the HVO. The celebration was a celebration. That was part of a protocol, and everybody is trying to be on their best behaviour and be very nice to each other, and you don't discuss any issues. You just have a drink and exchange niceties.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Let me rephrase my question. The first anniversary of the BH army and the celebrations about that, did they take place on the 14th or the 15th of April, 1993?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I don't know if it was on the 14th or a day or two, even earlier. But I know it wasn't later than the 14th. It could have been the 14th or before. It's possible that it was on the 14th, and it certainly wasn't on the 15th. So it was the 14th.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: All right. You mentioned the names of the two people whom you first conducted negotiations, Borislav Jozic and Mr. Zvonimir Cilic?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: These people with whom you had negotiated with, were they wearing military or civilian clothes?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: [No interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Both of them were members of the Vitez Brigade?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I assume.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Who was the commander?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: Mr. Mario Cerkez.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: When you said that they had received instructions to conduct negotiations with you, in your opinion, from whom had they received those instructions? From the military or from the civilian authorities?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Mr. Lopez-Terres, that's a matter of opinion on the part of the witness. No.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: This Boro Jozic, was he killed during the conflict?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I think he was killed.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you. One final question. On the 29th of April, 1993, while you were being detained, there was an agreement between the HVO authorities and those of the BH army, so that all of the prisoners would be released on the 30th of April, starting at noon. An order was issued by Colonel Blaskic to all brigades, including the one of the accused, Mario Cerkez. Do you know why you and other people among the important Muslims in the Muslim community were not released on that date, that is, the 30th of April?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: I can say that we were not released. What their plans were, that is difficult for me to say. We were not released. We stayed there.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: You were never able to get an explanation for that?

utterances.speaker: WITNESS K [Resumes]
utterances.text: There was no explanation.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. LOPEZ-TERRES
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I have no further questions.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Witness L, that concludes your evidence. Thank you for coming to the International Tribunal to give it. You are now released.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Scott.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, before we take the next witness, which we'll need to address some matters in private session, but even before that, if I could either ask the Court now, or I assume the Court would rather deal with it at the end of the day, I would like to save, if we can, a couple of minutes to deal with the release question. We're still not sure exactly what the Court's thinking on that, and the Prosecution has some questions procedurally about that. So if I could just alert the Court or ask the Court to reserve a couple of minutes at the end of the day, I would appreciate that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: Yes, we'll do that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SCOTT
utterances.text: Your Honour, the next witness -- if we can go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: I'm just going to have a word with the legal officer, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE MAY
utterances.text: 3.59 p.m., to be reconvened on Friday, the 16th day of September, 1999, at 9.30 a.m.
